t: how to hire an ecommerce website developer

inline: An ecommerce store has all the complexity of a general website plus the operational complexity of a retail business. A strong general developer can build a functional store; they often cannot build a store that sells well. The difference is not the design or the code quality — it is the ecommerce-specific knowledge that general developers usually lack.

blocks.text: What ecommerce adds that general websites do not have

items: Carts, checkout flows, order management, refunds, and returns.
Payment gateways, PCI compliance, tokenization, and 3D Secure.
Zones, rates, weight-based shipping, and tax calculations across regions.
SKU management, variants, and integration with ERP or PIM systems.
Product-heavy pages, image optimization, and caching strategies that work with WooCommerce or Shopify's model.
Every ecommerce developer should know what a good checkout completion rate looks like, and why.

inline: A general developer who has built ten content sites is not the same as an ecommerce developer who has built ten stores. The general developer may be technically excellent and still miss the specific details that make a store work — the checkout edge cases, the payment failure modes, the performance at scale. If your project is ecommerce, the "best" developer is almost always one with demonstrated ecommerce depth. For the general framework, see
These are the criteria that differentiate a strong ecommerce developer from a general developer with ecommerce experience. The general criteria from the
guide still apply — this page adds the ecommerce-specific depth.

blocks.text: 1. Platform depth, not just platform familiarity

inline: The developer should have built stores on your specific platform — not just used it, but built production stores on it at scale. A Shopify developer should be fluent in Liquid, Shopify APIs, and app ecosystem trade-offs. A WooCommerce developer should be fluent in PHP, WordPress hooks, and plugin conflict resolution. A headless developer should be fluent in React, Next.js, and Storefront API. For the platform comparison, see

t: Shopify vs WooCommerce vs custom builds

inline: Checkout is the highest-risk part of any store because bugs cost real revenue. The developer should be able to explain how they have handled payment gateway integration, PCI compliance, tax calculation, and failed-payment edge cases. A developer who treats checkout as part of "general QA" rather than as a dedicated phase is not an ecommerce developer — they are a general developer who has worked on a store. For a real example of what checkout work looks like, see

t: how a real checkout rebuild improved completion 21%

inline: Ecommerce sites are harder to make fast than content sites because product and checkout pages are heavier and caching is more complex. A strong ecommerce developer should be able to answer specifics: which caching layer, how they handle cart and checkout caching (which is usually excluded from full-page caching), what mobile load time they target, and how they keep the WooCommerce or Shopify database performant at scale. See

Every ecommerce store of any size needs integrations: ERP, CRM, accounting, email, inventory, and analytics. A strong developer should be able to describe specific integrations they have built and how they handled the data sync challenges. "We'll figure it out" is not an integration answer.

blocks.text: 5. Post-launch support for a live store

inline: A live ecommerce store has different post-launch needs than a content site. Checkout bugs cost revenue immediately, security incidents affect customer trust, and platform updates can break the store if they are not tested. A strong ecommerce developer should have a specific support arrangement, a same-day response time for critical issues, and a maintenance plan. See

sections.title: Platform Matters More Than People Think

inline: The single biggest cause of failed ecommerce hires is a developer whose expertise does not match your platform. A brilliant Shopify developer will struggle on a headless Next.js build, and vice versa. This is not a matter of intelligence — it is a matter of specific platform knowledge that takes years to build.

blocks.text: Why "any platform" claims are a red flag

inline: No one is genuinely deep in every platform. A developer who claims deep expertise in Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, headless, and custom builds is a generalist with shallow experience across all of them. The "best" ecommerce developer for your project is almost always one who has deliberately specialised in your platform. See

inline: Add the totals. For ecommerce, platform depth and checkout expertise are the two criteria that predict success most reliably. If a candidate scores below 3 on either, do not hire them regardless of their total score.

blocks.text: What a strong ecommerce score looks like

inline: A strong ecommerce developer typically scores 4 or 5 on all eight rows, with platform depth and reference quality highest. That pattern — where the developer's own ecommerce clients are the strongest evidence — is the clearest signal of a top-tier ecommerce developer.
These questions are specifically designed to test ecommerce depth. Ask them in this order.

b: "Which ecommerce platform do you specialise in, and how many stores have you built on it?"

items: A strong developer gives a specific number and platform. A weak developer claims to build on everything.

b: "Show me three live ecommerce stores you built. What was your specific role on each?"

items: A strong developer distinguishes solo builds from team contributions. A weak developer claims full credit for everything.

b: "How do you handle PCI compliance and payment tokenization?"

items: A strong developer explains tokenization, hosted checkout, and minimizing PCI scope. A weak developer is confused about what PCI actually means.

b: "Walk me through how you tested checkout before launch. What edge cases did you cover?"

items: A strong developer describes failed payments, coupon stacking, address validation, tax calculation, and multi-item orders. A weak developer says "we test everything."

b: "How do you approach caching on an ecommerce site, and how do you handle cart and checkout pages?"

items: A strong developer explains why cart and checkout pages cannot be cached like content pages. A weak developer gives a generic "we use caching" answer.

b: "What integrations have you built into an ecommerce store?"

items: A strong developer names specific systems (ERP, CRM, accounting, email) and describes the data-sync challenges. A weak developer says "we integrate with anything."

b: "What is your response time for a checkout outage?"

items: A strong developer gives a specific same-day answer. A weak developer says "we're flexible."

b: "What could go wrong on my project, and how would you handle it?"

items: A strong developer names specific risks and specific mitigations. A weak developer says "we don't expect any issues."

inline: Look at your brief. If your project is a standard template store with a small catalog and no integrations, a strong general developer who has built a few stores will do fine. If your project has any of the complexity factors above, hire an ecommerce specialist. The mistake is hiring a generalist for a project that needs a specialist — not the other way around. See

If you have three to five finalists who all score well on the framework above, the decision usually comes down to four tiebreakers. The tiebreakers are the same as the general framework, but weighted for ecommerce.

For ecommerce, this is the most predictive tiebreaker. A developer who has solved checkout problems on five similar stores is a better bet than one with broader experience but less checkout depth. Ask about their most complex checkout project and listen for specific edge cases.

blocks.text: Tiebreaker 2: Reference quality from similar stores

inline: A reference from a store similar to yours — same platform, similar scale, similar complexity — is worth more than three references from content sites. Ask for references whose projects most resemble yours.
A developer who can cite performance improvements on stores they have built is more likely to deliver a fast store than one who cannot. Ask for specific before-and-after numbers.

Checkout outages cost revenue by the hour. A developer with a same-day response time for critical issues is a stronger choice for ecommerce than one without a defined SLA, even if everything else is equal. See

blocks.text: What should not be a tiebreaker

items: A 20 percent price difference is small compared to the cost of a failed ecommerce launch. If a developer is dramatically cheaper than the others, that is worth examining, not celebrating.
A Shopify Partner badge is a weak positive signal; a "top developer" badge is usually pay-to-play. Neither replaces a live portfolio.
A developer who built one page for a famous brand is not necessarily better than one who built ten full stores for mid-market clients.

faqs.q: How do I find the best website developer for my ecommerce store?
a: Start with referrals from other ecommerce founders, then verify each candidate against the five ecommerce criteria above: platform depth, checkout expertise, performance, integrations, and post-launch support. Avoid generic "best developer" directories — they rarely reflect ecommerce-specific capability. See the

faqs.q: Is a Shopify developer better than a WooCommerce developer?
a: Neither is universally better — it depends on your platform. A Shopify developer is the right choice if you are on Shopify or Shopify Plus; a WooCommerce developer is the right choice if you are on WooCommerce. The mistake is hiring a developer who does not specialise in your platform. See

faqs.q: How much does the best ecommerce developer cost?
a: Rates vary widely. In the US, ecommerce developers typically charge $75 to $200 per hour; in India, ₹500 to ₹4,500. Platform specialists command a 10–30% premium. For the full cost breakdown, see

faqs.q: Do I need a specialist or can a general developer build my store?
a: It depends on your project. For a small template store with a standard catalog and no integrations, a strong general developer is fine. For anything with custom checkout, complex integrations, multi-currency, or high traffic, hire an ecommerce specialist. See

t: when a general developer is fine

faqs.q: What should I look for in an ecommerce developer's portfolio?
a: Three live ecommerce stores you can open on mobile and test the checkout yourself. Stores should be similar in scale and complexity to yours, not just aesthetically impressive. If the portfolio shows only content sites, they are not an ecommerce developer.

faqs.q: How long does it take to build an ecommerce store?
a: A small template store takes 6–10 weeks; a mid-market build with integrations takes 10–16 weeks; a headless or enterprise build takes 4–9 months. The timeline depends on scope, platform, integrations, and how quickly your team reviews and signs off. See

faqs.q: What is the biggest red flag when hiring an ecommerce developer?
a: "We test checkout as part of general QA." Checkout is the highest-risk part of the store and should be a dedicated QA phase with specific edge-case testing. A developer who does not treat it that way has not worked on enough stores to know where the real bugs are. See

faqs.q: Should I hire a local ecommerce developer or a remote one?
a: Not necessarily local. Local matters when you need timezone overlap, in-person kickoff or launch support, or the ability to verify the developer in person. For most ecommerce projects, remote is fine and often better value. See

faqs.q: How do I verify a developer's ecommerce results?
a: Ask for two references whose projects are similar to yours and for the live URLs of the stores in question. Open the stores yourself, run PageSpeed Insights on them, and ask the references specifically what changed. Claims without verification are marketing, not evidence. See
for what a real, verifiable case study looks like.

faqs.q: What is the most reliable vetting signal for an ecommerce developer?
a: Live ecommerce stores you can open on mobile and take through checkout yourself. A developer with three live, functional ecommerce stores is almost always a legitimate ecommerce developer. A developer with no live stores is not.

inline: Shortlist three to five ecommerce developers, score them on the framework above, and use checkout experience and reference quality as your tiebreakers. A structured comparison is the single most reliable way to avoid a bad ecommerce hire.
